newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia stocks buoyed by jobs weak data but end down.
newsitem.headline: Australia stocks buoyed by jobs weak data but end down.

text.p: The Australian share market almost wiped out all of its earlier losses on Thursday as bank stocks rebounded when long bond yields fell on hopes of a further rate cut following a weak set of June jobs data.

The All Ordinaries index was 1.7 points down at 2,694.4, after it dropped over 30 points at the opening following a 120 point plunge on Wall Street on Wednesday and on further weakness in the gold and copper prices.
Trade was a respectable A$800 million (US$600 million).

"The expectation of a rate cut is the main driving force in the market today," said Peter Morgan, equities manager at Perpetual Funds Management. Brokers said the weaker than expected June jobs data had set the scene for another rate cut.

Australian employment rose by just 11,900 in June, after a fall of 40,300 in May, but full-time employment fell 16,900 in June. The participation rate also fell, giving an unemployment rate of 8.5 percent, against 8.8 percent in May.
The increase in employment was well below median market forecasts of a 40,000 rise. The weak data sent bonds into a frenzy and the long bond yield fell more than 10 basis points.

The bond market rally fed into bank shares with the banking index, the largest sector on the Australian bourse, rising about 1.7 percent, led by strong rises in amongst Australia's big four banks NAB, ANZ, Commonwealth Bank and Westpac.
The Reserve Bank of Australia last cut interest rates on May 23 by 0.5 percentage points to 5.5 percent.

"The expectations are for another rate cut ... whether it is going to appear or not I don't know, because if you read Costello's comments he has a different view on the thing," Morgan said. Earlier Treasurer Peter Costello said the market should sit back and wait for previous cuts to take effect.
The banks rally pulled the industrial sector into the positive zone after spending most of the day in negative territory. But resources ended down on weaker gold and copper.
